mastery.oneLine: Hands-on spinal examination: PPIVMs test movement between vertebrae through natural bends; PAIVMs test small glides between them.
mastery.whatItIs: PPIVMs (Passive Physiological Intervertebral Movements) and PAIVMs (Passive Accessory Intervertebral Movements) are hands-on tests of how each spinal segment moves and whether it hurts. They help you decide where to treat. They are also used for mobilization.
mastery.analogy: Walking along a row of doors and pushing each one lightly: you note which one sticks, which one swings too freely and which one makes a squeaky sound that matches the patient's complaint.
coreIdeas: Pain response is more reliable than judging stiffness by feel. Ask what the patient feels at every level.
Always compare neighboring levels and think in three parts: how much it moves, how it feels and what it provokes.
A stiff segment does not prove it is the cause. Link what you find to the patient's comparable sign.

terms.meaning: Pushing a vertebra from back to front.
Central pushes on the spinous process in the midline. Unilateral pushes on one side near the facet.
Stiffer than expected / moving more than expected.
Reproducing the patient's pain during the test.
How consistently different examiners find the same result. For spinal stiffness, it is only fair, so link it to symptoms.

whenToUse: Back or neck pain where you want to find the most relevant segment.
Before choosing mobilization level and direction.
whenNot: Suspected fracture, instability or serious pathology (use medical assessment first).
Severe pain or irritability where testing would cause a flare.
Any neurological deficit that is progressing.

steps.title: Screen and ask about the pain
steps.detail: Know the pain area and the comparable sign before testing.

steps.title: Position
steps.detail: Example: prone with the spine in a neutral resting position for lumbar PAIVMs.

steps.title: Locate the segments
steps.detail: Palpate the spinous processes and identify levels accurately.

steps.title: Test central PA at each level
steps.detail: Press gently and rhythmically. Note stiffness, spring and pain at each level.

steps.title: Compare unilateral PA, then PPIVM
steps.detail: Repeat to the left and right and in bending directions if needed.

steps.title: Record and link
steps.detail: Record 'hypo/normal/hyper' and the pain response, then check whether treating that level improves the comparable sign.

mastery.dose: Assessment pressure is gentle and brief: a few oscillations per level. When used as treatment, follow the Maitland grading and dose guidance.

example.patient: Priya, 34, low back pain on bending forward after gardening.
example.assessment: Central PA at L4 reproduces her pain and feels stiffer than L3 and L5. Forward bending is limited by pain.
example.treatment: A Grade III central PA at L4 for 30 seconds, three sets, in prone.
example.reassess: Forward bending improves by several centimeters with less pain, which confirms L4 is relevant. If bending had not changed, you would search another level or direction.

mistakes: Trusting the feel of stiffness alone without linking to pain or function.
Testing at the wrong level through poor palpation.
Using too much force in an irritable spine.

selfTest.a: Pushing a vertebra from back to front.

selfTest.q: Which is more reliable, pain response or perceived stiffness?

mastery.recap: Test each level, ask about pain, and prove relevance by retesting.
mastery.evidence: Reliability of judging stiffness between examiners is limited, whereas reproducing the patient's pain is more consistent. These tests guide treatment but do not diagnose a structure.

depth.why: Passive physiological intervertebral movement (PPIVM) and passive accessory intervertebral movement (PAIVM) let the clinician feel stiffness, pain and end-feel at one segment. Reliability between examiners is modest, so the findings are used together with symptoms and other tests, not on their own.
choose: Use as a guide to which segment reproduces the patient's pain and which is stiff or hypermobile.
Combine with active movement and a neurological screen; do not treat a single stiff level in isolation.
Prefer outcome-based re-testing: the finding that matters is the one that changes with treatment.
parameters: central, unilateral and transverse pressure on the spinous or articular pillar, graded by force
pain provocation, stiffness grade and muscle guarding, compared with the neighbouring levels
the same segment before and after treatment, same pressure and position
depth.progress: As an assessment, progress means adding combined movements and functional tests to the segmental findings, then repeating the same tests after any treatment so the change is attributed to what was done.
measure: Stiffness compared with the level above and below
depth.evidence: Inter-examiner reliability for stiffness is low-to-moderate; pain provocation is more reliable. Use it to generate a hypothesis, then test the hypothesis.
pitfalls: Treating the stiff level only because it is stiff.
Using different positions before and after so the finding appears to change.
Over-reading a single test in a tense or guarded patient.
screen: The same screening as for any spinal manual therapy
Do not apply pressure over a suspected fracture, tumour or infection

urdu.short: PAIVM aur PPIVM spinal assessment ke tareeqay hain: PAIVM mein accessory pressure aur PPIVM mein spine ki physiological movement assess ki jati hai. Sirf palpation se kisi segment ko 'stuck' ya dard ki asal wajah kehna reliable nahi.

details.heading: Summary — khulasa
details.text: PAIVM aur PPIVM spinal examination ka hissa hain. Treatment ka faisla symptoms ke response par hona chahiye, sirf segmental diagnosis assume karke nahi.

details.heading: Science — source kya kehta hai
details.text: PAIVM mein central ya unilateral posterior-anterior jaisi controlled accessory force di jati hai; PPIVM mein spinal segments ke darmiyan passive physiological movement assess hoti hai. Segmental motion palpation ki stand-alone reliability aur diagnostic validity limited hai. Is liye history, neurological exam, active movement aur patient's comparable sign ke sath findings interpret karein. Behtar clinical use hypothesis test karna hai: kya controlled input symptoms ya movement ko reproduce, reduce ya meaningful taur par change karta hai?

details.heading: Procedure — tareeqa
details.text:
1. Segmental testing se pehle active movement, neurological status aur comparable sign note karein.
2. Patient ko relaxed position mein rakhein aur target level tak baghair unnecessary force ke pohanchein.
3. PAIVM ke liye graded central ya unilateral accessory pressure dein aur pain, resistance aur symptom distribution monitor karein.
4. PPIVM ke liye relevant physiological movement guide karte hue relative segmental motion palpate karein.
5. Sirf palpation par segment ko 'stuck' ya 'out of place' label na karein.
6. Treatment trial ke baad original comparable sign foran dobara check karein; technique tabhi retain karein jab useful change aaye.

details.heading: Dosage — miqdaar
details.text: Assessment mein symptom response aur movement behavior judge karne ke liye minimum force use karein. Therapeutic trial mein irritability ke mutabiq grade aur amplitude rakh kar 30–60 seconds ke 2–4 sets test kiye ja sakte hain. Dose palpated stiffness ke bajaye response-guided honi chahiye.

details.heading: Indications — source mein di gayi surat-e-haal
details.text: Mechanical spinal pain jahan comparable sign reproduce ho; painful ya restricted spinal movement jahan segmental treatment trial madadgar ho sakta ho; cervical, thoracic ya lumbar examination ka adjunct.

details.heading: Precautions — ehtiyati baatein
details.text: High irritability, osteoporosis ya fracture risk, recent trauma ya surgery, neurological symptoms, aur upper cervical presentations jahan specific vascular aur ligament screening zaroori ho.

details.heading: Contraindications — kab na karein
details.text: Suspected fracture ya instability, acute myelopathy ya progressive neurological deficit, region mein active infection ya malignancy, suspected cervical arterial pathology, ya koi presentation jise urgent medical assessment chahiye.

details.heading: Reassessment — dobara jaanch
details.text: Original comparable sign, active spinal range, symptom distribution, zaroorat par neurological status, aur patient ke liye meaningful functional task.

details.heading: Pearl — yaad rakhne wali baat
details.text: PAIVM/PPIVM findings clinical reasoning ka sirf ek hissa hain, apne aap mein diagnosis nahi. Examiner ko stiff mehsoos hone wala segment lazmi nahi ke pain ka source ho. Minimum effective manual input use karke gain ko active movement mein transfer karein.

details.heading: Misal — sirf samjhane ke liye
details.text: Farz karein back pain ke sath ek comparable movement limited hai. Clinician screening ke baad gentle segmental input se pehle aur baad us movement ko compare karta hai. Palpation ka ehsaas akela diagnosis nahi banta. Yeh illustrative example hai.

deeper.heading: Clinical reasoning
deeper.text: PAIVM aur PPIVM spinal assessment ke manual examination approaches hain. PAIVM mein therapist spinal segment par accessory movement assess karta hai, jabke PPIVM mein physiological movement ko passively examine kiya jata hai. Findings ko history aur neurological assessment ke saath interpret karein.

deeper.heading: Assessment ka purpose
deeper.text: Segmental mobility, symptom response aur movement quality clinical information de sakte hain, magar palpation ki reliability limited ho sakti hai. Comparable signs, patient comfort aur overall pattern ko priority dein; single finding se diagnosis final na karein.

deeper.heading: Safety aur common mistakes
deeper.text: Spinal assessment se pehle red flags, trauma, neurological changes aur relevant contraindications screen karein. Forceful testing, pain provoke karke repeat karna, ya uncertain segmental finding ko definitive lesion kehna avoid karein.

deeper.heading: Clinical interpretation
deeper.text: Assessment finding ko functional limitation aur management plan se link karein. Retest ka maqsad sirf segment ko 'feel' karna nahi, balkay symptoms aur movement ke meaningful change ko dekhna hai.

cue.wake: Your finger is a clinical tool. It is not a secret spinal X-ray.
cue.question: Two examiners feel different 'stiff levels.' Can either claim a vertebra is out?
cue.answer: Not from palpation alone. Combine reproducible function, history and screening.
cue.easy: PAIVM = passive small accessory spine movement; PPIVM = passive natural spine movement.

technique.storyHeadline: A spinal segment feels stiff. Is that enough to call it the problem?

episode.patient: Two clinicians examine the same lower-back region. One feels a stiff segment; the other isn't convinced. The patient simply wants to bend down without the familiar ache. That shared movement becomes the more dependable starting point.
episode.decision: PAIVMs and PPIVMs can explore accessory or physiological movement as one part of a wider examination. Neither technique alone proves that a vertebra is 'out of place.'
episode.retest: Return to bending and consider the complete clinical picture. If the segmental finding doesn't help explain a meaningful change, don't let it dominate the diagnosis.
episode.spark: A palpation finding is a clue, not a jury verdict.

aha.hook: A stiff-feeling segment is a clue, not a courtroom verdict.
aha.analogy: Your hands can ask useful questions about movement and symptom response, but one palpation finding does not get to declare a vertebra 'out of place.'
aha.challenge: Two clinicians disagree about which segment is stiff. What should guide the next decision?
aha.reveal: Use history, neurological examination, active movement and a reproducible comparable sign. Segmental palpation is one imperfect piece of the assessment.

weave.dialogue: Patient: 'So you can feel exactly which vertebra is out?' Clinician: 'I can explore movement and symptom response—but my thumb is not a spinal X-ray.'
weave.watch: One examiner supports the trunk and applies controlled accessory or physiological movement while observing the patient's response. Another clinician might perceive segmental stiffness differently. The familiar bend or turn is retested to place the palpation finding in context.
weave.method: PAIVMs and PPIVMs are structured examination inputs, not lie detectors for a vertebra. Use them alongside history, neurological screening, active motion and reproducible functional signs.
weave.science: Reliability of segmental motion palpation is limited as a stand-alone diagnostic method. A stiff-feeling segment does not prove a malpositioned vertebra or identify the sole source of pain.
weave.question: Two skilled examiners disagree about which segment is stiff. Is it reasonable to diagnose a displaced vertebra anyway?
weave.answer: No. Interpret the finding cautiously and prioritize a convergent clinical examination with reproducible comparable signs.
weave.closer: The thumb can contribute a clue. It cannot deliver the entire verdict.

patientPosition: Use prone, side-lying, sitting or supine according to the region and test. The patient must be relaxed enough that guarding does not dominate the finding.
Support the head, trunk and limbs so the target spinal region is exposed without unnecessary end-range positioning.
In cervical work, establish neurological, vascular and ligamentous safety before applying segmental force.
therapistPosition: Stand or sit so your shoulders stay relaxed and your body weight can control the force rather than isolated finger pressure.
Align yourself with the intended accessory or physiological movement so the force is precise and repeatable.
handPlacement: For PAIVM, contact the relevant spinous process, articular pillar or transverse process using a broad, anatomically safe contact.
For PPIVM, palpate adjacent segments while the other hand guides the physiological movement.
Avoid direct compression over superficial nerves, painful bony prominences, surgical sites or vulnerable tissue.
forceDirection: Central PAIVM: controlled posterior-to-anterior force through the selected spinous process.
Unilateral PAIVM: posterior-to-anterior force through the selected articular pillar or transverse process, modified for region and anatomy.
PPIVM: move the spine through the relevant physiological direction while judging relative motion and symptom response between adjacent segments.
Use lower amplitude within comfortable range for pain-dominant presentations and larger amplitude toward resistance only when stiffness dominates and safety is clear.
applicationSteps: 1. Record the comparable sign: pain, active range, symptom distribution or functional limitation.
2. Complete neurological and red-flag screening appropriate to the spinal region.
3. Position the patient and establish a comfortable contact at the suspected level.
4. Apply the lowest useful force and observe pain, resistance, guarding and any distal symptom behavior.
5. Compare adjacent levels only as clinically necessary; do not search for a single 'abnormal segment' as a diagnosis.
6. If a therapeutic trial is indicated, apply a short controlled set matched to irritability.
7. Retest the original comparable sign immediately.
8. Keep the technique only if it produces a meaningful, repeatable benefit and then reinforce the gain with active movement.
expectedResponse: Reduced pain, easier active movement, improved tolerance of the comparable sign or less guarding.
A useful response should be clinically relevant to the patient, not just a change in what the examiner feels.
stopCriteria: New or worsening distal neurological symptoms.
Dizziness, visual disturbance, drop attacks, severe headache or other vascular warning features during cervical work.
Sharp, severe or unfamiliar pain, marked guarding, or repeated worsening after each trial.
commonMistakes: Treating palpated stiffness as proof of a painful or dysfunctional segment.
Using excessive force to make the segment 'move'.
Ignoring poor reliability of stand-alone segmental motion testing.
Failing to compare the manual finding with active movement, neurological examination and function.
clinicalExample: Example: a patient has painful right cervical rotation without neurological deficit. After baseline screening, a low-grade unilateral PA trial at a clinically relevant level is applied. If rotation becomes easier immediately, the therapist follows with active rotation and motor-control work rather than repeatedly mobilizing the segment.

mechanism.mechanismMap: Controlled segmental pressure or passive movement → mechanical + sensory input → symptom provocation/modulation → hypothesis testing → active reassessment
mechanism.simpleExplanation: PAIVMs and PPIVMs are most useful when treated as clinical tests and treatment trials rather than as proof that one spinal segment is mechanically abnormal. The manual input loads local tissues and changes sensory input, which may alter pain and movement temporarily. The clinically important question is whether the patient's meaningful sign changes.
stepByStep: 1. A controlled accessory or physiological movement is applied.
2. Local skin, joint, muscle and periarticular receptors respond to the mechanical input.
3. The movement can reproduce, reduce or leave symptoms unchanged.
4. The therapist compares this response with active movement, neurological findings and function.
5. A short treatment trial may reduce pain or guarding through multisystem sensory and mechanical effects.
6. The original comparable sign is immediately retested.
7. The finding is retained only as part of the broader clinical hypothesis.
physiology: Accessory loading changes local mechanical stress and afferent input.
Pain modulation may occur through peripheral, spinal and supraspinal mechanisms.
Short-term changes in guarding and movement tolerance can occur.
Manual perception of segmental stiffness has limited stand-alone reliability, so it should not be overinterpreted.
clinicalTranslation: Use PAIVM/PPIVM to add information, not to replace history, neurological screening and active movement testing.
A positive treatment response is more clinically useful than simply finding a level that feels stiff.
When improvement occurs, move quickly into active movement and self-management.
myths: A palpably stiff segment is not proof that it is the pain generator.
The examiner cannot reliably identify a vertebra that is 'out of place' by PAIVM or PPIVM.
Manual treatment does not permanently reposition spinal segments.
mechanism.evidenceNote: Research on stand-alone segmental motion testing shows limited reliability and diagnostic validity. Use these techniques as part of a multi-factor clinical examination and judge treatment value by meaningful reassessment.

mechanismEvidence.summary: Manual therapy does not have one universal mechanism. Modern evidence supports interacting peripheral, spinal, supraspinal, neurovascular, neuromuscular and contextual responses. The exact mechanism responsible for a patient's clinical improvement is often uncertain.
mechanismEvidence.sourceTitle: The mechanisms of manual therapy: A living review of systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews

room.arrival: Two clinicians disagree about which spinal segment feels stiff. The patient only knows that bending is painful. Their familiar bend becomes the important reference point.
room.touch: Use controlled accessory or physiological movement as part of a broader examination. Palpation alone cannot prove a vertebra is displaced.
room.retest: Ask the person to bend again and weigh the finding with history, movement and neurological examination.
